title: Simple Past Tense
subtitle: Finished actions, and the -ed that marks them.
objectives: Form the simple past of regular verbs
Use the simple past for finished actions
Keep one tense across a whole sentence
Recognise the simple past in a text

cards.title: The simple past is for things that are over
cards.text: Not still happening. Not about to. Done, finished, in the bag — and usually with a time you could name.

cards.title: Regular verbs add -ed. That is it
cards.text: Most English verbs are regular, and regular means boring in a helpful way.
points: **walk → walked.** **train → trained.**
**Ends in e?** Just add -d: *race → raced*.
**Short vowel then one consonant?** Double it: *stop → stopped*.
**Ends in consonant + y?** Swap to -ied: *carry → carried*.

cards.title: Tap a pattern
cards.text: Four spelling rules cover every regular verb. The last two are where marks go.

question.text: Write the simple past of 'jog'. One word.
question.explain: Short vowel, single consonant, so the g doubles: jogged.

cards.title: A training log is written entirely in the past
cards.text: Every line of it is a finished action with a time attached.
points: **Monday: I skipped for twenty minutes.**
**I wrapped my hands before the bag work.**
**He corrected my guard twice.**
**All finished, all -ed.** That is what a log is.

cards.title: Words that force the past tense
cards.text: If one of these is in the sentence, the verb has to follow.
points: **yesterday, last night, an hour ago**
**in 2019, when I was nine**
**The marker and the verb must agree.**
*Yesterday I train* is wrong. *Yesterday I trained* is right.

options: Last night I fixed the fan.
Last night I will fix the fan.
Last night I fix the fan.
Last night I am fixing the fan.
question.explain: 'Last night' is finished time, so the verb must be simple past: fixed.

cards.title: Writing up what you did to something
cards.text: Open a fan, and the write-up afterwards is all simple past.
points: **I unplugged it first.**
**I unscrewed the guard and lifted the blade off.**
**The capacitor looked swollen.**
**I replaced it and the motor started.**

question.text: The simple past can describe something still going on now.
question.explain: That is what the present tense is for. Simple past means finished.

cards.title: Literature Review: Don Quixote, Chapter 11: The Adventure with the Barber
cards.text: Quixote sees a barber wearing his brass basin against the rain, and decides it is a legendary golden helmet.
points: **He charged the barber**, who ran and left the basin.
**Quixote claimed it** as the Helmet of Mambrino.
**Sancho said nothing**, because arguing never worked.
**Notice the verbs.** The whole chapter is simple past.

cards.title: Over, and nothing left running
cards.alt: An empty plate after a meal with used cutlery, crumbs and a drained glass
cards.text: That is the simple past. It happened, it finished, and it is not still going on.

terms.def: The tense for an action that is finished.
A verb that forms its past by adding -ed.
A word like yesterday that fixes when something happened.
Keeping the same tense across a sentence.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Simple past = finished action, often with a stated time.
Regular verbs add -ed, with three small spelling rules.
A past time marker forces a past verb.
Do not switch tense halfway through a sentence.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 1 English. The simple past is introduced as a meaning first — finished, usually with a stated time — and only then as a spelling rule, so -ed is a consequence rather than an arbitrary ending. The three spelling exceptions are given together because they are small and interfere with each other if met separately. Every freely chosen example sentence is from his world: a training log, a fan teardown, a lap. Tense agreement gets its own checkpoint since mid-sentence tense drift is the commonest error in his writing at this stage.
discussion: Why does 'yesterday' force the verb to change?
Which three spelling rules cover almost every regular verb?
How is a training log written, and why?
extension: Write five lines of a training log, all in the simple past.
Find ten -ed verbs in one page of Chapter 11.
misconceptions: Switching tense halfway through a sentence.
Doubling the final consonant when the vowel is long.
